records.summary: The project page describes a delta-wide sand budget combining field measurements, numerical modelling and stakeholder consultation. records.summary: On 2 February 2026 in Vientiane, partners in the WWF-Laos and Lao Academy of Social and Economic Sciences project "Safeguarding the Mekong: Advancing Sand Governance and Biodiversity Protection for Climate Resilience in Laos" held a roundtable to present initial research findings on sand mining policies and practices along the Mekong River and its tributaries in Lao PDR. The project is supported by the CARA initiative with UK FCDO funding. According to the article, initial findings and rapid assessments highlighted growing environmental pressures, including riverbank erosion, habitat degradation, biodiversity impacts and potential risks to community livelihoods. Next steps include continued research, awareness-raising, national dialogues, policy briefs and regional knowledge-sharing workshops.

records.title: From Tibet to the 'Nine Dragons', Vietnam's Mekong Delta Is Losing Sand
records.dateKind: Publication date stated in article body
records.dateEvidence: Source dateline: Jan. 13, 2019, at 7:45 p.m.
records.location: Mo Cay and Ben Tre province, Mekong Delta, Vietnam; Reuters visited three provinces straddling different branches of the delta
records.summary: Reuters reports that upstream damming and extensive riverbed sand mining are causing the land in the Mekong Delta to sink at around 2 cm (0.75 inches) a year, according to experts and officials. Riverbank erosion in Ben Tre province has destroyed homes, such as that of shopkeeper Ta Thi Kim Anh. Can Tho University expert Duong Van Ni says the problem is a lack of sediment and that since China built hydropower plants new sand almost never reaches the delta. The article says sand mining in Cambodia boomed over the last 10 years, partly driven by Singapore demand, and Cambodia banned all sand exports in 2017 under pressure from environmental groups. In Ben Tre, officials describe night-time illegal miners, and a local patrol group claims it got rid of 90 percent of thieves in the first few months, with none approaching since 2018. China's Foreign Ministry and Singapore's Ministry of National Development gave statements on downstream concerns and import controls respectively.
records.limitations: News report relying on attributed statements from officials, experts and locals; no quantified sand extraction volumes; subsidence cause attribution is general (dams and mining) and the 90 percent figure is a patrol member's claim. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

mergedLocalRecords.authors: Peijia Wang, Kaidao Fu, Jiangcheng Huang, Xingwu Duan and Zaizhi Yang
mergedLocalRecords.location: Jinghong to Guanlei reach, including Jinghongba and Ganlanba reaches, Yunnan, China
mergedLocalRecords.summary: Using multi-source satellite imagery (1993–2016) and a November 2018 field survey between Jinghong and Guanlei in Yunnan, the authors identified six sand-mining sites (three in Ganlanba, two large sites in Guanlei, and one in Jinghong halted after 2008). They report 1993–2016 erosion areas of 0.36 km² in Jinghongba and 0.33 km² (against 0.61 km² accretion) in Ganlanba, concluding that cascade dams reduced upstream sediment supply so sand-mining pits could not refill, accelerating bed deepening, particle coarsening and beach erosion.

records.title: Stop sand mining to save the Mekong Delta
records.dateKind: publisher datePublished metadata and body date
records.dateEvidence: Source dateline: 17/06/2017 11:35 GMT+7
records.location: Mekong Delta (ĐBSCL), Vietnam, including Tien River in Dong Thap, Vam Nao River in Cho Moi, An Giang, and Hau River
records.summary: Tuổi Trẻ reports on a workshop held 16 June organised by the Vietnam Hydraulic Association and the HCMC Hydraulic Science Association. Papers reportedly agreed on recommending an end to sand mining in the Mekong Delta; delegates said that without stopping it the delta would be in danger within a few decades. A Marine Engineering Institute report said that since 2005 erosion on the Tien River in Dong Thap has been intense; Đỗ Hoài Nam stated that 101 km of the 122.9 km main channel in Dong Thap is eroded, nearly 300 ha of bank land was lost in 2005-2016, and losses were estimated at about 320 billion dong. A 24 April landslide on the Vam Nao River in Cho Moi, An Giang, reportedly destroyed 16 houses. Scientists attributed erosion to flood flows, reduced sand from upstream Mekong structures, and excessive sand mining. Research data cited say sediment reaching the delta from upstream is only about 30 million tonnes per year, while licensed sand extraction (excluding illegal mining) is reportedly comparable. Some participants proposed a total ban, while others said only reduced extraction is feasible now because of high construction demand and no substitutes.
records.limitations: News report of workshop presentations; underlying studies are not detailed, and the sediment and mining figures are cited without methodology. Licensed mining volume is only said to be roughly equal to 30 million tonnes per year, with no separate exact figure. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

records.title: Intensified susceptibility to riverbed incisions under sand mining impacts in the Vietnamese mekong delta: A long-term spatiotemporal analysis
records.authors: Menna Farag Ahmed, Doan Van Binh, Sameh A. Kantoush, Edward Park, Nguyen Luyen Phuong Doan, Anh Tuan Luc, Nguyen Dinh Vuong, Thi Huong Vu, Binh Quang Nguyen, Anh Ngoc Trieu, Xuan Tung Nguyen and Tetsuya Sumi
records.dateEvidence: Article states available online 27 November 2024; volume 470 issue date 1 February 2025.
records.location: Vietnamese Mekong Delta channels
records.summary: Analyzing bathymetric datasets across the Vietnamese Mekong Delta from 1998 to 2020, the authors estimate net annual incision volumes of −119 million m³/year (1998–2005), −69 million m³/year (2005–2017) and −66 million m³/year (2017–2020), with local incision reaching up to −13 m/year during 2017–2020. They estimate that licensed sand mining’s contribution to annual net riverbed incision rose from 27.7% in 2005–2017 to 35.3% in 2017–2020.
records.limitations: Repository abstract read. The 27.7% and 35.3% attribution figures refer to licensed sand mining relative to net incision; unlicensed extraction and upstream sediment starvation also affect the delta.

records.title: Mekong River dry season changes due to hydropower dams and extractive processes: Making sense of contradictory community observations in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia
records.authors: Ian G. Baird, Michael A.S. Thorne and Sirasak Gaja-Svasti
records.dateEvidence: Article header lists Water Alternatives Volume 18, Issue 3 (2025), pp. 521–545; exact day not printed in the article PDF
records.studyPeriod: Focus group interviews in 44 villages (1 March–3 April 2024), follow-up interviews in May–June 2024 and May–June 2025, and gauge records spanning 1923–2023
records.location: 32 villages across 8 Thai provinces (Chiang Rai to Ubon Ratchathani), 9 villages in Champasak (Lao PDR), and 3 villages in Stung Treng (Cambodia)
records.summary: Combining March–April 2024 focus groups across 44 Mekong villages in Thailand, Lao PDR and Cambodia with gauge and sediment records, the authors explain why 17 sandy-substrate villages between Nong Khai and Mukdahan perceived lower dry-season water levels despite dam releases increasing dry-season discharge. They link the perceived drop to riverbed incision from upstream sediment trapping, bank embankments (83% of the Thai bank versus 12–13% of the Lao bank) and sand mining, noting Thai–Lao rules barring mining within 1,000 m of embankments and a Vientiane operator’s report that post-monsoon sand accumulation fell from 6 m in the early 1990s to 80 cm.
records.limitations: Full article read. The authors note that neither Thailand nor Lao PDR collects public totals of actual sand volumes extracted, and their analysis cannot quantitatively separate mining-driven incision from dam-driven hungry-water incision.
records.retrieval: Full article read
records.editorialStatus: Source reviewed; owner review pending

records.title: Dammed in the Mekong: Averting an Environmental Catastrophe
records.dateEvidence: Report header and dateline: Report 343 / Asia-Pacific, 07 October 2024
records.studyPeriod: Interviews conducted June 2022–January 2024; historical and projected basin data to 2050/2100
records.location: Mekong basin (excluding Myanmar in field interviews)
records.summary: Crisis Group Asia Report No. 343 examines the cumulative governance, ecological and human-security risks of hydropower (661 operational dams) and sand mining across the Mekong basin. Its sand-mining analysis cites delta extraction averaging 43 million m³/year (2015–2020)—14 to 17 times natural replenishment—and 2007–2016 Cambodia-to-Singapore trade discrepancies (nearly 3 million tonnes reported exported versus >80 million tonnes reported imported), alongside 585 delta erosion hotspots spanning >740 km. It recommends integrating sand-mining monitoring into the MRC’s Core Monitoring Function and National Mekong Committees.
records.limitations: Policy synthesis report based on literature review and 2022–2024 interviews; quantitative sand-mining and erosion figures are cited from published studies and Vietnamese authorities rather than new field measurements, and Myanmar was excluded from fieldwork.

records.authors: Sepehr Eslami, Piet Hoekstra, Herman W. J. Kernkamp, Nam Nguyen Trung, Dung Do Duc, Hung Nguyen Nghia, Tho Tran Quang, Arthur van Dam, Stephen E. Darby, Daniel R. Parsons, Grigorios Vasilopoulos, Lisanne Braat, Maarten van der Vegt

records.studyPeriod: January–April 2016 (field campaign 1–9 April 2016); 2008 vs. 2018 bathymetry comparison

records.summary: Eslami et al. records.title: Intensifying saline water intrusion and drought in the Mekong Delta: From physical evidence to policy outlooks
records.authors: Ho Huu Loc, Doan Van Binh, Edward Park, Sangam Shrestha, Tran Duc Dung, Vu Hai Son, Nguyen Hoang Thu Truc, Nguyen Phuong Mai, Chris Seijger
records.dateEvidence: Sci Total Environ. 2021 Feb 25:757:143919. Epub 2020 Dec 3 Date supplied by Gemini; independent date verification is pending.
records.location: 11 gauge stations across the Vietnamese Mekong Delta
records.summary: Applying spectral analysis and rating-curve diagnostics to multi-decadal hourly-to-daily water-level and salinity records at 11 VMD stations, this study documents up to 66% tidal amplification and rating-curve slope shifts. It shows that riverbed sand mining incises delta channels by up to 15 cm/yr, intensifying backwater effects and saltwater intrusion alongside upstream dams, sea-level rise, and land subsidence.
records.limitations: Gauge-based spectral and rating-curve analyses capture aggregate channel deepening without isolating individual illegal mining pits. The study discusses combined drivers and does not isolate individual mining operations.

records.originalTitle: Mining the Mekong: Land and Livelihoods Lost to Cambodia’s Thirst for Sand
records.dateEvidence: Source dateline: Story August 29, 2022
records.location: Roka Koang commune, Kandal province, on the Mekong River, Cambodia; also the Bassac River
records.summary: Pulitzer Center story (supported by its Rainforest Investigations Network) reports that residents of Roka Koang commune, Kandal province, blame sand mining by politically connected companies for riverbank collapses on the Mekong that have cost them homes and fishing-based livelihoods. The Cambodian government, via Ung Dipola of the Ministry of Mines and Energy, denies that dredging causes erosion and says it helps stabilise the banks; University of Newcastle and University of Southampton researchers call this "a myth". According to the Ministry of Mines and Energy, Cambodia has 49 active licenses covering 2,320 hectares of the Mekong and Bassac rivers, and 11.7 million m3 of sand was extracted in 2020 and 11.5 million m3 in 2021, with 6.1 million m3 in the first six months of 2022. Dipola said only around 4% of the river is licensed for dredging. Hackney's research suggested extraction exceeded natural replenishment by almost five times in 2018 and by a factor of 16 in 2020. Echo-sounder surveys by Leyland and Darby found extraction scars routinely 5 m deep and one barge taking roughly 9,450 m3 in a day. The researchers warn that riverbed lowering could affect the Tonle Sap reversal of flow. The article also describes company ownership links to political elites, including Global Green Energy Development, Jin Ling Construction and Sophearoth Aphivath, and says the government has not released the environmental impact assessments.

records.title: Sand mining in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta sinks homes, livelihoods and hopes
records.originalTitle: Sand mining in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta sinks homes, livelihoods and hopes
records.dateEvidence: Source dateline: Published Nov 22, 2023, 01:00 PM
records.location: Can Tho city and Hau Giang province, Mekong Delta, southern Vietnam
records.summary: AFP reports that shoreline erosion linked to sand mining and upstream hydropower dams threatens hundreds of thousands of people in Vietnam's Mekong Delta, with homes collapsing into the Hau river in Can Tho and Hau Giang. It cites a WWF report and a 2018 WWF-led Mekong River Commission study saying sediment could fall by up to 97 per cent by 2040. Government figures show at least 750km of riverbank and nearly 2,000 houses sank into rivers between 2016 and August 2023. Vietnam's Ministry of Transport says the delta needs 54 million cubic m of sand for six highways before 2025 and the river system can supply less than half. Mekong expert Nguyen Huu Thien says that at an extraction rate of 35 million to 55 million cubic m a year, sand would run out by 2035. State media report over US$470 million spent on 190 anti-erosion projects since 2016, and officials cite around 20,000 households needing resettlement, while WWF says half a million could lose homes. Alternatives such as sea sand or Cambodian imports are being debated, and projects have been delayed.
records.limitations: News report; figures are attributed to WWF, the MRC-linked study, ministries, and state media and are not independently verified here; no specific mining site data; Hau river is the only named river. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

records.summary: Newcastle University describes research led by Dr Chris Hackney using high-resolution satellite imagery and underwater sonar to map sand mining in the Mekong. According to the research, tracking vessels over a stretch of the Mekong for 2016–2020 showed extraction rose "from 24 million tonnes a year to 59 million tonnes", which is "sixteen times greater than the amount of sand the river is naturally transporting itself", resulting in a negative sand budget and widespread riverbed lowering. The article says this disturbs breeding grounds for fish and invertebrates, can increase salinity intrusion in the Mekong delta and can increase riverbank erosion. Sonar maps show craters "up to 8 m deep" and "up to 70 m in diameter", and comparing 2022 with 2013 surveys indicates the riverbed is in some places "more than 10m lower". Earlier research said a "three meter lowering" would make much of the banks unstable. The team hopes the data inform better regulation and monitoring in Cambodia and other impacted regions.

records.title: Sand mining threatens Asia’s largest lake
records.originalTitle: Sand mining threatens Asia’s largest lake
records.dateEvidence: Publisher page metadata: 2025-11-10
records.location: Mekong near Phnom Penh and Tonlé Sap lake, central Cambodia
records.summary: The article reports a new Nature Sustainability study led by Quan Le (Loughborough University) that links sand mining-induced riverbed lowering in the Mekong to a weaker Tonlé Sap flood pulse. Le says modelling shows "a clear relationship between sand mining—induced riverbed lowering and the reduction of the Tonlé Sap's flood pulse." One simulation found that if mining continues at its current pace, "by 2038 the flood pulse volume will decline by 69% and the wet season size of Tonlé Sap lake will shrink by 40%," and "dry season outflows to the Mekong delta will drop by 59%." The authors call sand mining "an existential threat" to the lake and say the only effective mitigation is to halt and reverse riverbed lowering. An earlier 2021 study by Ng and Park blamed dredging near Phnom Penh. The article says officials in Cambodia and Viet Nam have banned sand export, but Le says Cambodia still meets rising domestic demand by dredging the Mekong.
